title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 3.4.1 Writing: Mechanics of Writing (Handwriting)

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Handwriting is clear when another person can read it at once. In this sub-strand you will print lower-case and capital letters neatly, watch the difference between b and d, copy polite phrases, and spell words with silent letters, blends and double consonants.

## Strand 3.0: Etiquette
Sub-strand 3.4.1: Writing: Mechanics of Writing (Handwriting)
Suggested lessons: 3

## What this sub-strand covers
• Legibility
• Neatness
• Spelling

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 3.0 Etiquette, Sub-strand 3.4.1 Mechanics of Writing: Handwriting

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) write legibly and neatly in print script for clarity of communication
b) apply accurate and consistent spelling in print script for writing fluency
c) adopt the use of accurate and consistent spelling in a variety of print scripts for effective communication

## Key inquiry questions
1. How does being unable to read other people’s work make you feel?
2. Why should you ensure your written work is easy to read?

PAGE 2: How we will learn

## Learning experiences
• use appropriate writing instruments (pencil first and then a pen) to copy a simple text
• print lower and upper case letters neatly and legibly
• pay attention to consistent letter size and height, direction of strokes such as dots, tails, crossbars, curves and differences in letter orientation like ‘d and ‘b
• write silent letters in words and phrases such as ‘please listen’ ‘I beg your pardon’, ‘may I borrow your watch’
• look up words and find the correct spelling from a digital device with peers
• consistently use the correct spelling of words with blends and double consonants

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: This is enhanced as the learner writes words legibly, neatly and spells them correctly.
• Learning to learn: This is developed as the learner builds on their writing skills by paying attention to consistent letter size and height, direction of strokes such as dots, tails, crossbars, curves and differences in letter orientation.

## Values
• Love: It is shown as the learners work harmoniously with peers to look up words and find the correct spelling from a digital device.
• Responsibility: It is enhanced as the learner uses the digital devices appropriately to look up words and find correct spelling.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Self-esteem: This is developed as learner gains confidence in writing legibly and neatly.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the concept of writing legibly and neatly in Kiswahili.

PAGE 3: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print

LESSON 1: LEGIBLE AND NEAT PRINT
================================

## What you will learn
• Print small, tall and tail letters at a consistent size.
• Form b and d so they face the right way.
• Copy a short polite sentence neatly in pencil.

Curriculum outcomes: a) write legibly and neatly in print script for clarity of communication

## Introduction
A kind message fails if the reader cannot tell your letters apart. Neat print is part of courtesy. The person who reads your note should not have to guess whether you wrote b or d.

## Notes

### Print script
Print script means each letter stands on its own. The letters are not joined. Start with a pencil so you can form the letters lightly. When the shapes are steady, you may copy the same line with a pen.

Sit up, put the paper straight in front of you, and leave a margin. Hold the pencil so you can see the point. Leave a space about the width of the letter o between words.

PAGE 4: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print — Three heights

### Three heights
Think of a line the letters sit on.

- Small letters stay in the middle height: a, c, e, i, m, n, o, r, s, u, v, w, x, z. The dot of i sits above the letter.
- Tall letters rise above that height: b, d, h, k, l and t.
- Tail letters drop below the line: g, j, p, q and y.

Capital letters are tall. They sit on the line and do not grow tails. A, B, C and the rest of the capitals should match one another in height. Do not let one capital tower over the next.

Keep the same size across a line. A small a should not suddenly become as tall as an l.

PAGE 5: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print — b and d

### Strokes that must be there
- Dots on i and j. A missing dot can make i look like l.
- The crossbar on t and on f. Without it, t can look like l.
- Tails on g, j and y, long enough to see but not so long that they crash into the line below.
- Curves on c, o, a, e and s, closed where they should be closed. An open o can look like a u.

### b and d
These two letters cause the most mix-ups.

- b has the stick on the left and the round part on the right.
- d has the round part on the left and the stick on the right.

A memory that helps: in the word bed, b and d face each other, like the two ends of a bed. Write bed slowly and check the direction.

p and q need the same care. p has the tail on the left and the round part on the right. q has the round part first and the tail on the right.

PAGE 6: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print — A sentence to copy

### A sentence to copy
Copy this in pencil, then check every tall letter and every tail:

Please listen. May I borrow your pen?

If a letter is wrong, do not scribble it out. Draw one light line through it and write the letter again above or beside it, as your teacher prefers. The page should still look calm.

PAGE 7: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print — Key words

## Key words
• print script — writing in which each letter stands separately
• legible — clear enough for someone else to read
• crossbar — the horizontal stroke on t or f
• tail — the part of a letter that goes below the line

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner's i looks like l. What stroke is missing?

Working:
1. The letter i is a small letter plus a dot.
2. Without the dot it resembles a tall or small stick.

Answer: The dot

## Worked examples

### Example 2
How can you check that b and d in the word bed are facing the right way?

Working:
1. b has its stick on the left.
2. d has its stick on the right.
3. In bed the two round parts face the e in the middle.

Answer: The sticks are on the outside and the round parts face the e, like the ends of a bed.

PAGE 8: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print — Answers to practice

## Activity: Pencil copy on the line
You will need: A pencil, Lined paper, The sentence Please listen. May I borrow your pen?

1. Print a line of small letters, a line of tall letters and a line of tail letters. Keep each group the same height.

2. Print the capitals A to H at one height.

3. Write the word bed three times and check b and d.

4. Copy the polite sentence in pencil. Leave spaces between words and a margin.

5. A partner reads your sentence aloud. If they hesitate, reshape the unclear letter.

## Practice

1. Name three tail letters.

2. What is missing if t looks like l?

3. Describe how b is different from d.

4. Why do we start a neat copy in pencil?

## Answers to practice

1. Any three of g, j, p, q and y.

2. The crossbar.

3. b has the stick on the left and the round part on the right. d has the round part on the left and the stick on the right.

4. So we can form the letters lightly and correct the shape before we use a pen.

## Summary
• Small, tall and tail letters each have their own height.
• Dots, crossbars, tails and curves must be visible.
• In the word bed, b and d face each other.

PAGE 9: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Copy with your eyes and your ear

LESSON 2: COPYING POLITE PHRASES AND SILENT LETTERS
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Copy polite phrases legibly in print.
• Spell words that contain a silent letter or a tricky spelling.
• Keep letter size steady when you write a whole line.

Curriculum outcomes: a) write legibly and neatly in print script for clarity of communication; b) apply accurate and consistent spelling in print script for writing fluency

## Introduction
Please listen. I beg your pardon. May I borrow your watch? These polite phrases are short, but a missing letter or a wandering tall letter makes them hard to trust. Copying them trains both your hand and your spelling.

## Notes

### Copy with your eyes and your ear
Read the phrase aloud, then write it, then read what you wrote. The three steps catch different mistakes. The ear may notice a missing word. The eye may notice a letter facing the wrong way.

Phrases to copy:

- Please listen.
- I beg your pardon.
- May I borrow your watch?

Write them first in pencil. When the line is even, write them again in pen. Do not press so hard that the pen tears the page. Keep capitals for Please, I and May, because each of those words starts a sentence. Watch begins with a small w here because it is not starting the sentence.

PAGE 10: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Letters you must not drop

### Letters you must not drop
Some words hide a letter when we speak.

- listen: the t is silent. We say the word without a clear t, but we still write l-i-s-t-e-n. A common mistake is to write lisen.
- please: the letters e and a together make the vowel. Write p-l-e-a-s-e. Leaving out the a gives plese, which is not the word.
- pardon: say every letter as you learn the spelling, p-a-r-d-o-n. Do not write parden.
- borrow: there are two r letters in the middle, b-o-r-r-o-w. One r is not enough.
- watch: the ending tch is the spelling of the last sound. Write w-a-t-c-h. Do not stop at wash or wach.

PAGE 11: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Looking up a spelling

The t in listen is a true silent letter. In watch, t is part of the spelling tch even though you do not hear a separate t. Either way, the letter has to be on the page.

### A dictation line
Ask a partner to read this once while you listen, then once more while you write:

Please listen. I beg your pardon. May I borrow your watch?

Check silent t, the a in please, the double r in borrow, and the question mark at the end. May I is a question, so the last phrase needs a question mark.

### Looking up a spelling
If you are unsure, look the word up with a partner on a dictionary your teacher has approved, in a book or on a device. Type or find the word, read the spelling, then cover it and write it from memory. Check once more. Using a device for spelling is useful. Wandering onto other pages is not the task. Stay with the dictionary until the word is copied correctly into your book.

Neatness and spelling work together. A perfectly spelled word that cannot be read still fails. A beautiful letter that is the wrong letter fails too.

PAGE 12: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Example 1

## Key words
• silent letter — a letter that is written but not sounded, such as t in listen
• dictation — writing words that someone else reads aloud
• question mark — the sign ? used at the end of a question

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner writes "Please lisen." What is missing, and why is it easy to miss?

Working:
1. The correct spelling is listen.
2. The t is not clearly heard, so writers leave it out.

Answer: The silent t is missing. Listen is spelled l-i-s-t-e-n.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Which ending punctuation does "May I borrow your watch" need?

Working:
1. May I asks for permission.
2. A question ends with a question mark.

Answer: A question mark.

## Activity: Copy, then check the hidden letters
You will need: Pencil and pen, Lined paper, A dictionary, print or digital, with the teacher's guidance

1. Copy the three phrases in pencil, keeping tall letters even.

2. Underline the silent t in listen, the a in please, the double r in borrow and the tch in watch.

3. Write the same phrases in pen.

4. With a partner, dictate the phrases and mark any missing letter.

5. Look up one word you are unsure of and write it again from memory.

PAGE 13: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Summary

## Practice

1. Spell the word in which t is silent: the word that means to pay attention with your ears.

2. Write the phrase that asks permission to use someone's watch.

3. What two letters sit together in the middle of borrow?

4. Why do you read a phrase aloud before you copy it?

## Answers to practice

1. listen

2. May I borrow your watch?

3. rr (a double r)

4. So you hear every word and are less likely to leave one out.

## Summary
• Copy polite phrases in even print, in pencil and then in pen.
• Write the silent t in listen and the full spellings of please, borrow and watch.
• A question that begins with May I ends with a question mark.

PAGE 14: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling

LESSON 3: BLENDS, DOUBLE CONSONANTS AND STEADY SPELLING
=======================================================

## What you will learn
• Spell words that begin or end with consonant blends.
• Spell words with double consonants correctly.
• Use the same correct spelling each time you write the word.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply accurate and consistent spelling in print script for writing fluency; c) adopt the use of accurate and consistent spelling in a variety of print scripts for effective communication

## Introduction
Please starts with two consonant sounds said together. Sorry keeps a double r every time you write it, not only on the first try. Steady spelling is what makes your print fluent instead of full of repairs.

PAGE 15: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Blends

## Notes

### Blends
A blend is two or three consonant sounds said together, each one still heard. It is not the same as a silent letter. In a blend, you hear the consonants.

- pl in please
- br in borrow
- fr in friend
- gr in greet
- sp in speak
- st at the end of guest
- sm in smile

When you print a blend, write both letters close in the word but still clear. Please needs p and l at the start. Guest needs s and t at the end. Dropping one letter of a blend makes a different word or a non-word: please without l looks like pease, and guest without s is not the word we want.

Say the blend as you write it, quietly: pl, br, fr. The mouth reminds the hand.

PAGE 16: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Double consonants

### Double consonants
A double consonant is the same consonant written twice. You usually hear it once, so the second letter is easy to forget.

- sorry: s-o-r-r-y
- manners: m-a-n-n-e-r-s
- little: l-i-t-t-l-e
- happy: h-a-p-p-y
- letter: l-e-t-t-e-r
- borrow: b-o-r-r-o-w
- better: b-e-t-t-e-r

Welcome has one l and one m. It is not wellcome. Learn that exception on purpose.

A pattern that often helps: after a short vowel, the consonant is doubled before an ending such as -y or -er in words like happy, letter and better. It is a pattern, not a promise about every word. When you are unsure, check a dictionary and then use that spelling every time.

PAGE 17: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Consistent means every time

### Consistent means every time
If you spell sorry correctly in the title and sory in the next line, the reader hesitates. Choose the right spelling and stay with it through the whole piece.

A short courtesy note to copy and keep consistent:

Dear friend,
Please smile and greet our guest.
I am sorry I forgot my manners.
May I borrow a little time to write a better letter?
Thank you.

Check pl, gr, st, the double letters in sorry, manners, little, better and letter, and the single l in a word like welcome if you add it.

### Keep the habit
Accurate spelling in print is a habit you adopt, not a trick you use once. Each time you write please, listen, borrow, sorry and friend, write them the same correct way. Your hand learns the movement, and your reader gets a clear message. That is writing fluency: the words come out neatly and correctly because you have practised them.

PAGE 18: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Example 1

## Key words
• blend — two or three consonants said together, each one heard, such as pl in please
• double consonant — the same consonant written twice, as rr in sorry
• consistent — the same correct form every time

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which letters make the blend at the start of please and at the start of borrow?

Working:
1. Please begins with p and l, both heard.
2. Borrow begins with b and r, both heard.

Answer: pl in please and br in borrow

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Correct the spellings in this line: I am sory. Please grete our gest.

Working:
1. Sorry has a double r.
2. Greet has ee and ends with t. The blend gr stays.
3. Guest ends with the blend st and has u.

Answer: I am sorry. Please greet our guest.

PAGE 19: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Spell, check and copy the note

## Activity: Spell, check and copy the note
You will need: Pencil and pen, Lined paper, A dictionary approved by the teacher

1. List the blends in please, borrow, friend, greet, speak, guest and smile. Say each blend aloud.

2. Write sorry, manners, little, happy, letter, borrow and better. Underline the double consonants.

3. Look up any word you doubt, with a partner, and correct it before the final copy.

4. Copy the short courtesy note in neat print. Use the same spelling every time a word repeats.

5. Exchange books. Read the note aloud. If you stumble, the writer fixes the letter or the spelling.

PAGE 20: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Answers to practice

## Practice

1. Write please, greet and guest, and name the blend in each.

2. Correct: sory, happy is already correct, litle, wellcome.

3. Why is welcome not spelled with a double l?

4. What does consistent spelling mean?

## Answers to practice

1. please (pl), greet (gr), guest (st)

2. sorry, happy, little, welcome

3. Welcome has one l. Doubling it is a common mistake, so we learn this spelling on purpose.

4. Using the correct spelling of a word every time you write it.

## Summary
• A blend keeps every consonant you hear, such as pl, br and st.
• Double the consonant in sorry, manners, little, happy, letter and better.
• Use the correct spelling every time so your print is fluent and clear.

PAGE 21: Revision quiz

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which letters drop below the line?
   A. a, c, o
   B. b, d, h
   C. g, j, y
   D. A, B, C

2. In the word bed, where is the stick of the letter b?
   A. On the right
   B. On the left
   C. Below the line
   D. Above a tail

3. What is missing when t looks like l?
   A. A dot
   B. A crossbar
   C. A tail
   D. A second t

4. Which spelling shows the silent letter correctly?
   A. lisen
   B. listen
   C. lissen
   D. listn

5. Which phrase is written correctly?
   A. may i borrow your watch
   B. May I borrow your watch?
   C. May I borow your wach
   D. May I borrow your watch

6. How many r letters are in the middle of borrow?
   A. One
   B. Two
   C. Three
   D. None

7. Which word begins with the blend pl?
   A. borrow
   B. please
   C. guest
   D. smile

8. Which spelling is correct?
   A. wellcome
   B. welcome
   C. welcom
   D. wecome

9. Correct this line: I am sory I forgot my maners.

10. Why should spelling stay the same each time you write a word?

PAGE 22: Quiz answers

ANSWERS
=======

1. C. g, j, y
   g, j and y are tail letters. They go below the line.

2. B. On the left
   b has the stick on the left and the round part on the right.

3. B. A crossbar
   The crossbar is the stroke that makes t different from l.

4. B. listen
   The t in listen is silent, but it must still be written.

5. B. May I borrow your watch?
   It is a question, so it needs a capital M and a question mark, and borrow and watch are spelled fully.

6. B. Two
   Borrow is spelled with a double r.

7. B. please
   Please begins with the consonant blend pl.

8. B. welcome
   Welcome has one l, not a double l.

9. I am sorry I forgot my manners.
   Sorry has rr and manners has nn.

10. So the reader trusts the word and your writing stays fluent and clear.
   Consistent spelling is part of writing that communicates.

================================

- d has the round part on the left and the stick on the right.

A memory that helps: in the word bed, b and d face each other, like the two ends of a bed. Write bed slowly and check the direction.

p and q need the same care. p has the tail on the left and the round part on the right. q has the round part first and the tail on the right.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print — A sentence to copy
studyPages.body:
### A sentence to copy
Copy this in pencil, then check every tall letter and every tail:

Please listen. May I borrow your pen?

If a letter is wrong, do not scribble it out. Draw one light line through it and write the letter again above or beside it, as your teacher prefers. The page should still look calm.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print — Key words
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• print script — writing in which each letter stands separately
• legible — clear enough for someone else to read
• crossbar — the horizontal stroke on t or f
• tail — the part of a letter that goes below the line

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner's i looks like l. What stroke is missing?

Working:
1. The letter i is a small letter plus a dot.
2. Without the dot it resembles a tall or small stick.

Answer: The dot

## Worked examples

### Example 2
How can you check that b and d in the word bed are facing the right way?

Working:
1. b has its stick on the left.
2. d has its stick on the right.
3. In bed the two round parts face the e in the middle.

Answer: The sticks are on the outside and the round parts face the e, like the ends of a bed.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Legible and neat print — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Pencil copy on the line
You will need: A pencil, Lined paper, The sentence Please listen. May I borrow your pen?

1. Print a line of small letters, a line of tall letters and a line of tail letters. Keep each group the same height.

2. Print the capitals A to H at one height.

3. Write the word bed three times and check b and d.

4. Copy the polite sentence in pencil. Leave spaces between words and a margin.

5. A partner reads your sentence aloud. If they hesitate, reshape the unclear letter.

## Practice

1. Name three tail letters.

2. What is missing if t looks like l?

3. Describe how b is different from d.

4. Why do we start a neat copy in pencil?

## Answers to practice

1. Any three of g, j, p, q and y.

2. The crossbar.

3. b has the stick on the left and the round part on the right. d has the round part on the left and the stick on the right.

4. So we can form the letters lightly and correct the shape before we use a pen.

## Summary
• Small, tall and tail letters each have their own height.
• Dots, crossbars, tails and curves must be visible.
• In the word bed, b and d face each other.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Copy with your eyes and your ear
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: COPYING POLITE PHRASES AND SILENT LETTERS
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Copy polite phrases legibly in print.
• Spell words that contain a silent letter or a tricky spelling.
• Keep letter size steady when you write a whole line.

Curriculum outcomes: a) write legibly and neatly in print script for clarity of communication; b) apply accurate and consistent spelling in print script for writing fluency

## Introduction
Please listen. I beg your pardon. May I borrow your watch? These polite phrases are short, but a missing letter or a wandering tall letter makes them hard to trust. Copying them trains both your hand and your spelling.

## Notes

### Copy with your eyes and your ear
Read the phrase aloud, then write it, then read what you wrote. The three steps catch different mistakes. The ear may notice a missing word. The eye may notice a letter facing the wrong way.

Phrases to copy:

- Please listen.
- I beg your pardon.
- May I borrow your watch?

Write them first in pencil. When the line is even, write them again in pen. Do not press so hard that the pen tears the page. Keep capitals for Please, I and May, because each of those words starts a sentence. Watch begins with a small w here because it is not starting the sentence.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Letters you must not drop
studyPages.body:
### Letters you must not drop
Some words hide a letter when we speak.

- listen: the t is silent. We say the word without a clear t, but we still write l-i-s-t-e-n. A common mistake is to write lisen.
- please: the letters e and a together make the vowel. Write p-l-e-a-s-e. Leaving out the a gives plese, which is not the word.
- pardon: say every letter as you learn the spelling, p-a-r-d-o-n. Do not write parden.
- borrow: there are two r letters in the middle, b-o-r-r-o-w. One r is not enough.
- watch: the ending tch is the spelling of the last sound. Write w-a-t-c-h. Do not stop at wash or wach.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Looking up a spelling
studyPages.body:
The t in listen is a true silent letter. In watch, t is part of the spelling tch even though you do not hear a separate t. Either way, the letter has to be on the page.

### A dictation line
Ask a partner to read this once while you listen, then once more while you write:

Please listen. I beg your pardon. May I borrow your watch?

Check silent t, the a in please, the double r in borrow, and the question mark at the end. May I is a question, so the last phrase needs a question mark.

### Looking up a spelling
If you are unsure, look the word up with a partner on a dictionary your teacher has approved, in a book or on a device. Type or find the word, read the spelling, then cover it and write it from memory. Check once more. Using a device for spelling is useful. Wandering onto other pages is not the task. Stay with the dictionary until the word is copied correctly into your book.

Neatness and spelling work together. A perfectly spelled word that cannot be read still fails. A beautiful letter that is the wrong letter fails too.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• silent letter — a letter that is written but not sounded, such as t in listen
• dictation — writing words that someone else reads aloud
• question mark — the sign ? used at the end of a question

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner writes "Please lisen." What is missing, and why is it easy to miss?

Working:
1. The correct spelling is listen.
2. The t is not clearly heard, so writers leave it out.

Answer: The silent t is missing. Listen is spelled l-i-s-t-e-n.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Which ending punctuation does "May I borrow your watch" need?

Working:
1. May I asks for permission.
2. A question ends with a question mark.

Answer: A question mark.

## Activity: Copy, then check the hidden letters
You will need: Pencil and pen, Lined paper, A dictionary, print or digital, with the teacher's guidance

1. Copy the three phrases in pencil, keeping tall letters even.

2. Underline the silent t in listen, the a in please, the double r in borrow and the tch in watch.

3. Write the same phrases in pen.

4. With a partner, dictate the phrases and mark any missing letter.

5. Look up one word you are unsure of and write it again from memory.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Copying polite phrases and silent letters — Summary
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Spell the word in which t is silent: the word that means to pay attention with your ears.

2. Write the phrase that asks permission to use someone's watch.

3. What two letters sit together in the middle of borrow?

4. Why do you read a phrase aloud before you copy it?

## Answers to practice

1. listen

2. May I borrow your watch?

3. rr (a double r)

4. So you hear every word and are less likely to leave one out.

## Summary
• Copy polite phrases in even print, in pencil and then in pen.
• Write the silent t in listen and the full spellings of please, borrow and watch.
• A question that begins with May I ends with a question mark.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: BLENDS, DOUBLE CONSONANTS AND STEADY SPELLING
=======================================================

## What you will learn
• Spell words that begin or end with consonant blends.
• Spell words with double consonants correctly.
• Use the same correct spelling each time you write the word.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply accurate and consistent spelling in print script for writing fluency; c) adopt the use of accurate and consistent spelling in a variety of print scripts for effective communication

## Introduction
Please starts with two consonant sounds said together. Sorry keeps a double r every time you write it, not only on the first try. Steady spelling is what makes your print fluent instead of full of repairs.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Blends
studyPages.body:
## Notes

### Blends
A blend is two or three consonant sounds said together, each one still heard. It is not the same as a silent letter. In a blend, you hear the consonants.

- pl in please
- br in borrow
- fr in friend
- gr in greet
- sp in speak
- st at the end of guest
- sm in smile

When you print a blend, write both letters close in the word but still clear. Please needs p and l at the start. Guest needs s and t at the end. Dropping one letter of a blend makes a different word or a non-word: please without l looks like pease, and guest without s is not the word we want.

Say the blend as you write it, quietly: pl, br, fr. The mouth reminds the hand.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Double consonants
studyPages.body:
### Double consonants
A double consonant is the same consonant written twice. You usually hear it once, so the second letter is easy to forget.

- sorry: s-o-r-r-y
- manners: m-a-n-n-e-r-s
- little: l-i-t-t-l-e
- happy: h-a-p-p-y
- letter: l-e-t-t-e-r
- borrow: b-o-r-r-o-w
- better: b-e-t-t-e-r

Welcome has one l and one m. It is not wellcome. Learn that exception on purpose.

A pattern that often helps: after a short vowel, the consonant is doubled before an ending such as -y or -er in words like happy, letter and better. It is a pattern, not a promise about every word. When you are unsure, check a dictionary and then use that spelling every time.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Consistent means every time
studyPages.body:
### Consistent means every time
If you spell sorry correctly in the title and sory in the next line, the reader hesitates. Choose the right spelling and stay with it through the whole piece.

A short courtesy note to copy and keep consistent:

Dear friend,
Please smile and greet our guest.
I am sorry I forgot my manners.
May I borrow a little time to write a better letter?
Thank you.

Check pl, gr, st, the double letters in sorry, manners, little, better and letter, and the single l in a word like welcome if you add it.

### Keep the habit
Accurate spelling in print is a habit you adopt, not a trick you use once. Each time you write please, listen, borrow, sorry and friend, write them the same correct way. Your hand learns the movement, and your reader gets a clear message. That is writing fluency: the words come out neatly and correctly because you have practised them.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• blend — two or three consonants said together, each one heard, such as pl in please
• double consonant — the same consonant written twice, as rr in sorry
• consistent — the same correct form every time

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which letters make the blend at the start of please and at the start of borrow?

Working:
1. Please begins with p and l, both heard.
2. Borrow begins with b and r, both heard.

Answer: pl in please and br in borrow

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Correct the spellings in this line: I am sory. Please grete our gest.

Working:
1. Sorry has a double r.
2. Greet has ee and ends with t. The blend gr stays.
3. Guest ends with the blend st and has u.

Answer: I am sorry. Please greet our guest.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Spell, check and copy the note
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Spell, check and copy the note
You will need: Pencil and pen, Lined paper, A dictionary approved by the teacher

1. List the blends in please, borrow, friend, greet, speak, guest and smile. Say each blend aloud.

2. Write sorry, manners, little, happy, letter, borrow and better. Underline the double consonants.

3. Look up any word you doubt, with a partner, and correct it before the final copy.

4. Copy the short courtesy note in neat print. Use the same spelling every time a word repeats.

5. Exchange books. Read the note aloud. If you stumble, the writer fixes the letter or the spelling.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Blends, double consonants and steady spelling — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Write please, greet and guest, and name the blend in each.

2. Correct: sory, happy is already correct, litle, wellcome.

3. Why is welcome not spelled with a double l?

4. What does consistent spelling mean?

## Answers to practice

1. please (pl), greet (gr), guest (st)

2. sorry, happy, little, welcome

3. Welcome has one l. Doubling it is a common mistake, so we learn this spelling on purpose.

4. Using the correct spelling of a word every time you write it.

## Summary
• A blend keeps every consonant you hear, such as pl, br and st.
• Double the consonant in sorry, manners, little, happy, letter and better.
• Use the correct spelling every time so your print is fluent and clear.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which letters drop below the line?
   A. a, c, o
   B. b, d, h
   C. g, j, y
   D. A, B, C

2. In the word bed, where is the stick of the letter b?
   A. On the right
   B. On the left
   C. Below the line
   D. Above a tail

3. What is missing when t looks like l?
   A. A dot
   B. A crossbar
   C. A tail
   D. A second t

4. Which spelling shows the silent letter correctly?
   A. lisen
   B. listen
   C. lissen
   D. listn

5. Which phrase is written correctly?
   A. may i borrow your watch
   B. May I borrow your watch?
   C. May I borow your wach
   D. May I borrow your watch

6. How many r letters are in the middle of borrow?
   A. One
   B. Two
   C. Three
   D. None

7. Which word begins with the blend pl?
   A. borrow
   B. please
   C. guest
   D. smile

8. Which spelling is correct?
   A. wellcome
   B. welcome
   C. welcom
   D. wecome

9. Correct this line: I am sory I forgot my maners.

10. Why should spelling stay the same each time you write a word?

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. C. g, j, y
   g, j and y are tail letters. They go below the line.

2. B. On the left
   b has the stick on the left and the round part on the right.

3. B. A crossbar
   The crossbar is the stroke that makes t different from l.

4. B. listen
   The t in listen is silent, but it must still be written.

5. B. May I borrow your watch?
   It is a question, so it needs a capital M and a question mark, and borrow and watch are spelled fully.

6. B. Two
   Borrow is spelled with a double r.

7. B. please
   Please begins with the consonant blend pl.

8. B. welcome
   Welcome has one l, not a double l.

9. I am sorry I forgot my manners.
   Sorry has rr and manners has nn.

10. So the reader trusts the word and your writing stays fluent and clear.
   Consistent spelling is part of writing that communicates.
